newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea buys corn for North, plans more food aid.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea buys corn for North, plans more food aid.

text.p: South Korea has bought 50,000 tonnes of corn and is considering more donations to hungry North Korea, which is facing probably the most difficult months in years of economic decline, Seoul officials said on Monday.

The state-run Agricultural and Fishery Marketing Corp said it bought the corn from China at $151.80 per tonne at a weekend tender for delivery by the end of next month to North Korea's western port of Nampo, near Pyongyang.
The corn is part of the $16 million in food aid that Seoul has pledged in response to an appeal by the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) for $95.5 million to stave off famine in the North.
About 300 tonnes of powdered milk will be shipped this month, while corn/soybean blend worth $6 million has already arrived in the North, the officials said.

The South Korean Red Cross was awaiting a response from its North Korean counterpart to a weekend proposal for further talks aimed at arranging more relief supplies in addition to another 50,000 tonnes of food being shipped by southern civic groups, a Red Cross spokesman said.
"Civic groups have promised more donations and we could offer tens of thousands of tonnes of more food to the North," he said.

Seoul's Deputy National Unification Minister Lee Ho said North Korea still needed donations of at least 400,000 tonnes of grain to last it until the next harvest in October if each citizen is to receive the minimum calorie requirements.

Lee said that amount was based on the assumption that all of the estimated 1.22 million tonnes already in stock in North Korea were made available for consumption. The grain stock -- as of end June -- was kept partly by the military, farmers and in black markets, he added.
"The North rationed an average of 350 grams of grain to its citizens between last November and June, although some people ate well over the minimum-required amount," he told Reuters.
Lee, who is in charge of analysing North Korean affairs, said corruption and an inefficient distribution system caused some North Koreans starve to death and many others suffer from malnutrition.
"This is not just because of floods in 1995 and 1996. Since 1990, it has been suffering from a chronic food shortage of between 1.5 million and two million tonnes annually," he said.
Seoul officials said that even with a bumper harvest this year, the Stalinist North would be short of at least one million tonnes of grain next year.
International aid agencies are stepping up food appeals for the North, warning of imminent starvation, particularly among young children who are most at risk.
The Rome-based WFP launched a fresh appeal last week for $46 million in food aid for the North on top of the earlier request for $95.5 million.

Washington, which has given $25 million to the WFP so far this year, and Seoul have said they are considering the latest WFP appeal. But they maintain that large-scale assistance will have to wait until Pyongyang begins peace talks.

Pyongyang has agreed to an August 5 meeting in New York of senior officials from the two Koreas, the United States and China to arrange four-nation talks on a peace treaty to replace the truce that ended the fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War but, technically, not the war itself.
